newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss leader confident gold foundation to get nod.
newsitem.headline: Swiss leader confident gold foundation to get nod.

text.p: Swiss President Arnold Koller was quoted on Saturday as saying he was confident voters would back a bold plan to create a humanitarian foundation that would sell official gold reserves to help victims of poverty and catastrophes.

Critics have blasted the plan as a misguided giveaway of national wealth to appease critics who accuse Switzerland of cynically profiting from World War Two. They have urged Swiss voters to block the idea in a referendum next year.

Koller said in an interview approval of the seven billion Swiss franc ($4.8 billion) Solidarity Foundation hinged on convincing Swiss the foundation was part of the country's humanitarian tradition and that money would be spent wisely.

"It is clear that there is still a lot of work to do to inform and persuade people. The circle of recipients in Switzerland and abroad must also be clearly defined, as well as the mechanism for handling the gold," he told the Journal de Geneve newspaper.
"But I am confident. The initial reaction has been positive for the most part."

Opinion polls show most Swiss back the plan -- which Koller unveiled in a speech to parliament this month -- to use part of Switzerland's vast but undervalued gold reserves to finance aid to the poor and victims of disasters and human rights outrages.
Koller said he had received around 400 letters suggesting ways the foundation could spend the roughly 350 million Swiss francs it would distribute each year, half in Switzerland and half abroad.
"We have received a lot of ideas. Someone told me, for example, it would be possible to eradicate leprosy on the panet with the amount of money envisaged," he said.
The foundation could also provide quick help to victims of natural disasters by cutting through red tape, he said.

"We want to have very spontaneous assistance without bureaucracy. We will certainly also have talks with the ICRC," he said, referring to the Swiss-based International Committee of the Red Cross, which Berne already helps finance.
Koller dismissed suggestions the foundation plan aimed to buy off neutral Switzerland's critics, especially those who condemn its close wartime economic ties to Nazi Germany.
"This is not at all a question of buying something, but of giving new content to our tradition of solidarity," he said.

He also made clear the foundation was not designed solely to help victims of the Holocaust, although they too might qualify. A separate fund financed by banks and private businesses will deal exclusively with Holocaust victims, he said. $ = 1.45 Swiss Francs)
